prize_parts.citation: for the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, using reversibly terminated fluorescent nucleotides on clustered single molecules

statement.case_for: After the full exchange my preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part, B011, credited to Balasubramanian and Klenerman. The reason is the one I gave in round 1 and that the discussion has not weakened. The decisive step is a chemical invention, a reversible 3'-blocked nucleotide with a cleavable fluorophore that lets a polymerase add exactly one base per cycle, combined with reading clustered single molecules in parallel. It is simple, it was a game-changer, and its consequences are fully realised and independently confirmed over about twenty years. Round 1 showed that no other configuration is near five: eight different first parts and no ballot with more than two explicit supporters. In that situation I should not move toward whichever candidate has a few more names behind it, but ask which candidate best survives the objections that were actually raised. B011 survives them best: its maturity is not disputed by anyone, and its attribution is the cleanest on the table. The remaining question, chemistry versus medicine, is a matter of citation wording, which I address below by crediting the nucleotide chemistry and single-molecule clustering rather than the field.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my position is the one Chabes and Linke both press, that sequencing is a platform and medicine achievement whose commercial history is entangled across Solexa, Lynx and 454, and that earlier prizes (1980, 1993) already touched DNA sequencing and PCR. I take it seriously. A two-name credit leaves out Rothberg, Mayer and Ju, and I cannot settle those priority claims from the files; my recollection is that the chemistry and cluster concepts credited to Cambridge were the route that came to dominate, but a careful expert report could change the credit. A second argument is that a one-part prize concentrates the whole outcome on a single candidate that only two of eight members preferred, which is a weak position from which to reach five votes.

responses.point: Chabes accepts that reversible-terminator chemistry is a real chemical invention and the Balasubramanian-Klenerman attribution is clean, but asks whether the committee is rewarding the chemistry or the platform engineering that followed, and notes the 1980 and 1993 prizes.
responses.response: This is the right question and I answer it by the wording of the citation, which names reversibly terminated fluorescent nucleotides on clustered single molecules and not instruments or throughput. The 1980 prize rewarded Sanger and Gilbert for chain-termination and chemical cleavage methods and the 1993 prize rewarded PCR and site-directed mutagenesis; neither rewarded cyclic, one-base-per-step synthesis with a reversible terminator read on a surface. That is a different chemical idea. On your own first choice, I accept the mechanism in B034 is sound, but whether Handa's cereblon work is part of the same achievement is exactly the open attribution dispute, and with no approved degrader I still think it is a year or more early. I would rank it above base editing as an alternative.

responses.point: Linke now adopts the two-person Cambridge pair, insists 454 pyrosequencing is chemically distinct and asks whether omitting it can be defended, and pairs it with a nanopore part credited to Bayley alone.
responses.response: I can defend omitting 454 because its pyrosequencing detects pyrophosphate release by luciferase and was not the chemistry that became the standard; the citation specifies the mechanism so that it does not claim the whole field. I would still ask the experts to confirm that, since I said it rests on recollection. On the second part, I do not support B001 credited to Bayley alone: you and several others have shown that Kasianowicz, Branton (deceased), Deamer, Akeson and Bayley each carry part of the credit, and a one-name part would invite a priority dispute. I would rather leave nanopores for a later prize than force an attribution now. I am also not persuaded that two sequencing-related parts make a more coherent prize than one.

responses.point: Aili prefers Crews and Deshaies for degraders paired with Liu alone for base editing, and says that excluding Kondo and Nishida is a credit judgement that Liu should address.
responses.response: I agree that excluding Kondo and Nishida is a judgement, not a settled fact, and I would not support B012 until the expert reports have been checked on their independent cytidine editing. Even setting that aside, the adenine editor and the systematic engineering are Liu's group's work, so I see Liu alone as the likelier outcome, but the clinical safety record is still short and the 2020 prize makes timing awkward. That keeps B012 as an alternative for me and not a part of my configuration. I also do not think combining two newer chemical-biology topics reaches the maturity standard that a single mature part does.

responses.point: Somfai prefers Buchwald and Hartwig for C-N coupling, defends it against the 2010 overlap, and pairs it with Liu alone.
responses.response: I thank you for taking my overlap argument seriously, and I agree with you that C-N coupling needed a different mechanistic solution from the C-C couplings of 2010. That makes B053 more defensible than I first allowed, and I now regard it as a credible mature candidate. What holds me back is Kosugi's earlier tin-amide coupling, which I cannot verify from the files, and the fact that only two members have ranked it. If the expert reports show Kosugi's work was not general and ligand-controlled catalysis was the real advance, I would be willing to put B053 higher, but I would not trade it for a pairing with base editing.

uncertainties: Priority among Solexa, Lynx and 454, and whether Rothberg, Mayer or Ju must be credited, still rests on my recollection and should be checked against the expert reports
Whether the committee accepts reversible-terminator sequencing as chemistry once the citation names the nucleotide chemistry, which is the only serious objection I see
Whether a single-part prize with only two round-1 supporters can reach five votes, and which alternative (B034 or B012) a majority could accept if it cannot
statement.conflict_note: No conflict. My Warshel EVB, ligand-binding and Uppsala ribosome work do not touch B011, B034 or B012, and I have no ties to any of the credited names. This is unchanged from round 1.
